nameStory: The salmon aeolis gets its name from its beautiful salmon-pink to orange coloration that resembles the flesh of a freshly caught salmon. The word 'aeolis' comes from the ancient Greek god of wind, Aeolus, referring to the flowing, wind-like projections called cerata that cover these sea slugs' backs.
description: The salmon aeolis is a type of sea slug called a nudibranch - essentially a snail that has lost its shell and developed colorful, finger-like projections on its back. These marine creatures are soft-bodied and typically display gorgeous salmon-pink to orange hues that make them stand out against the seafloor. Like other nudibranchs, they're carnivorous and move by gliding along surfaces using their muscular foot. They're part of a group called aeolid nudibranchs, distinguished by their numerous finger-like projections called cerata.

idTips.label: Salmon-pink coloration
idTips.description: Body displays distinctive salmon-pink to orange coloration that's reminiscent of salmon flesh, making it easily distinguishable from other sea slugs

idTips.label: Finger-like cerata
idTips.description: Back is covered with numerous soft, finger-like projections called cerata that feel gel-like to the touch and can be retracted when disturbed

idTips.label: Smooth, slimy texture
idTips.description: Body feels slippery and mucus-covered, similar to touching the inside of a raw oyster or clam

idTips.label: Two prominent tentacles
idTips.description: Head bears two horn-like tentacles called rhinophores that are often darker than the body and can be pulled back into sheaths

idTips.label: Gliding movement
idTips.description: Moves smoothly across surfaces using wavelike contractions of its muscular foot, leaving a faint slime trail

habitat: Found in cold New England waters, typically on rocky bottoms or among kelp forests and other seaweed beds. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are usually spotted in subtidal zones where their preferred prey - small hydroids and other cnidarians - are abundant.

seasonality.spring: May become more active as water temperatures begin to rise, though still require diving or very low tides to observe in shallow areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak observation season when warmer waters make diving more comfortable and the animals are most active in their feeding and reproductive behaviors.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may begin moving to deeper waters as temperatures start to drop, making surface observations less likely.
seasonality.winter: Least likely to be observed as they retreat to deeper, more stable temperatures and reduced diving activity limits human encounters.

funFact: Salmon aeolis can actually steal the stinging cells from the jellyfish and hydroids they eat, storing them in the tips of their finger-like projections to use as their own weapons - essentially becoming living thieves that turn their prey's defenses into their own protective arsenal!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other pink or orange nudibranchs, but the distinctive salmon-pink color combined with the finger-like cerata projections helps distinguish it. Remember: 'Salmon colored, salmon named' - if it looks like salmon flesh, you're probably looking at a salmon aeolis.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gill' in Latin, referring to how these sea slugs breathe through exposed gills or projections rather than being protected inside a shell like their snail relatives. Many people are surprised to learn that these colorful creatures are actually closely related to common garden snails.
compareHints: Since this is the only Ziminella species recorded in New England waters, compare it to other aeolid nudibranchs in the region by focusing on the distinctive salmon-pink coloration. Other aeolids may have similar finger-like projections but typically show different color patterns - whites, purples, or different shades of orange. The consistent salmon-flesh color is the key distinguishing feature of this particular species.
